## Background

Steamboat Hills has a fairly long geochemistry record for a Great
Basin system. White and coworkers mapped and characterized it
geologically and hydrologically starting in the 1950s-60s, and there's
a run of gas and water chemistry papers from the 1970s-90s: Nehring
(1979, 1980) on reservoir temperature and gas composition, Mariner and
Janik (1995) with water and gas analyses for several CPI production
wells -- well 23-5 among them, which ends up being our main comparison
point below -- and Arehart, Coolbaugh, and Poulson (2003) arguing for
a magmatic heat source from trace elements and gas geochemistry. I've
spent most of this project building a database that pulls all of this
together with NDEP, NDWR, and our own field data, mostly for the
chloride side of the thesis. But it means we actually have a real,
if sparse, historical gas-chemistry baseline to check new samples
against, which turned out to matter a lot for what follows.

## The 2025 eruption and the fissure

In June 2025 the Lower Sinter Terrace had a geyser-like eruption that
opened a new fissure -- Lindsey et al. (2026) give the fuller account
of how the activity built over 2022-2025 before that happened. The
well was capped not long after, but the discharge didn't stop; it just
moved laterally along the fracture system, and the fissure has kept
degassing and discharging since. Cary and I put together a poster on
this for GRC (Irvin and Lindsey, 2026), arguing mostly from paired
temperature loggers and a Cl mass-balance estimate that this looks
more like redistribution within an existing shallow conduit system
than a brand-new source turning on. The gas data below is the first
real test of that idea from a completely different angle.

## Sampling

You, Tobias, and Karim collected three gas samples at and around the
fissure on April 29-30, 2026: two points right at the fissure and a
third across the road at a separate degassing spot.

| Sample | Date | Approx. location | Field temp (C) | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| NV26-1 | Apr 29 | at the fissure | 99.5 | co-located with a water sample we collected May 1 (see below) |
| NV26-2 | Apr 30 | fissure, second point | 96 | flagged -- possible bottle leak noted in the field, also the point where sampling broke through fresh asphalt that the gas was escaping through |
| NV26-3 | Apr 30 | across the road | 96 | second degassing area |

NV26-2 is the one I most want your read on. We're not throwing it
out, but we're not treating it the same as the other two either, at
least not until we hear back on whether the leak and/or the asphalt
breakthrough would meaningfully change the result.

## What we're seeing so far

This is exploratory. Three samples, one of them flagged, so everything
below is a first look, not a result I'd want to lean on hard yet.

**Air correction and geothermometry.** Surface gas is never air-free,
so before doing anything else we corrected for atmospheric
contamination -- the standard approach: treat all measured O2 as air,
subtract air-derived N2 using the dry-air N2/O2 ratio, renormalize
everything else. All three samples have a real amount of air mixed in,
which isn't surprising for shallow vent sampling rather than a
wellhead, but NV26-2 turns out to be essentially explainable by air
alone.

| Sample | Air fraction (O2-based) | D'Amore-Panichi T (C) |
|---|---|---|
| NV26-1 | 53% | 228 |
| NV26-2 | 100% | 209 (not trusted -- see above) |
| NV26-3 | 64% | 181 |

Mariner and Janik's well 23-5 T-DP values from the 1990s run
173-200 C, so NV26-1 and NV26-3 bracket that range, and both sit well
above the measured field temperatures (96-99.5 C) -- the same pattern
already showing up in the water geothermometers, where quartz reads
below measured temperature and Na/K reads above it. A reasonable
result. Three samples still isn't much to build a conclusion on.

```{r fig-ratios}
#| echo: false
#| results: asis
img <- gsub("\\\\", "/", file.path(normalizePath(getwd()), "output", "figures", "gas_analysis", "gas_ratio_historical_comparison.png"))
knitr::asis_output(sprintf("![](%s)", img))
```

**How the two "good" samples compare to Nehring and to Mariner &
Janik.** CO2/N2, H2S/CO2, N2/Ar, and CH4/CO2 for NV26-1 and NV26-3 land
closer to Nehring's (1980) spring samples than to well 23-5, which
makes sense -- Nehring sampled surface springs too, not a wellhead, so
a similar degree of air mixing isn't a surprise. NV26-2 sits off on
its own in every panel, again consistent with it being mostly air.
Nehring and Mariner & Janik only overlap with us on major-gas
composition; neither reports a helium isotope ratio, so that
comparison stops at CO2/H2S/N2/Ar/CH4.

**A ternary view of the same thing.** The classic way to look at an
air-mixing question like this is an N2-He-Ar diagram -- the same style
Mariner & Janik use in their own Figure 9. I plotted our three points
against well 23-5, the two usable Nehring rows, and real dry air for
reference.

```{r fig-ternary}
#| echo: false
#| results: asis
#| message: false
#| warning: false
tern_path <- file.path(root, "output", "figures", "gas_analysis", "gas_ternary_n2_he_ar.png")
build_gas_ternary_diagram(con, out_png = tern_path)
img2 <- gsub("\\\\", "/", normalizePath(tern_path))
knitr::asis_output(sprintf("![](%s)", img2))
```

All three of our points, and both of Nehring's spring samples, cluster
right next to the air point. Well 23-5 sits noticeably further away,
toward more N2 relative to Ar and He, which lines up with the air
correction above -- surface vent and spring gas looks a lot more
air-like than gas collected at a wellhead. Not a new idea, but it's
nice to see it fall out of the data this cleanly. I used the common
He-times-100/Ar-times-10 scaling to make the plot readable; I haven't
gone back to a primary Giggenbach reference to confirm that's the
right scaling, or where the "real" air/crustal/mantle field boundaries
are supposed to sit on a plot like this, so that's flagged as a
question below rather than presented as settled.

**Helium isotopes -- there's a real 1982 baseline, and it's a
surprisingly tight match.** I'd first written this section saying
nobody had ever published a He-3/He-4 ratio for Steamboat. Wrong --
and I'm glad whoever caught that did, because the real source turned
out to be better than what I'd patched it with the first time.
Torgersen and Jenkins (1982, GCA) measured He isotopes in both water
and gas at four Steamboat springs. The two gas samples they
themselves call more reliable (Springs 6 and 10) both come out at
Rc/Ra = 6.0. Our three new samples come out at 5.6-6.0. That's about
as close a match as you could ask for across 44 years, and it's a
gas-to-gas comparison specifically, which matters, since their own
water-phase numbers run lower (3.9-4.5) and two of their gas values
are flagged in their own text as suspect (air mixing, or the vent
contaminating itself). See the figure below. Kennedy and van Soest
(2007, Science) -- which is actually where I first found this, via
Dhakal et al.'s citation of it, before going back and reading the
primary paper myself -- also names Steamboat as a high-R/Ra Basin and
Range site, but that's a regional paper, not Steamboat-specific.
Torgersen and Jenkins is the real, direct comparison. Arehart et al.
(2003) make basically the same magmatic-source argument from trace
elements and gas geochemistry, but cite a different, earlier Kennedy
paper (2002, not the 2007 one) and don't give a gas composition table
or a He number of their own, so they're interpretive context here
rather than a number to compare against.

```{r fig-heisotope-rup}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| results: asis
he_path <- file.path(root, "output", "figures", "gas_analysis", "he_isotope_historical_comparison.png")
build_he_isotope_historical_comparison(con, out_png = he_path)
img5 <- gsub("\\\\", "/", normalizePath(he_path))
knitr::asis_output(sprintf("![](%s)", img5))
```

Panel A above is the He-isotope comparison. Panel B is the closest
thing I can show for 2026, since we don't have a dissolved-gas/He
measurement on the water side this time -- it's the gas vs. water
temperature geothermometer comparison at this same NV26-1/SBF_0001
point instead. The pattern rhymes even though the measurement is
different: in 1982 every spring's gas phase reads a higher Rc/Ra than
its own water phase, and in 2026 the gas geothermometer reads hotter
than every water method except Na/K. Different quantity, same
qualitative story -- the gas phase is consistently telling you
something deeper and hotter than the water at the same point, in both
eras.

NV26-1 sits right on top of SBF_0001, a water sample we collected two
days later (May 1) with full major-ion and isotope chemistry -- a
mature Na-Cl thermal water, Cl 815 mg/L. It's the first spot in the
project with both phases from essentially the same location, which
matters more for the mixing modeling below than for anything already
covered above.

## How NV26-1, NV26-2, and NV26-3 relate to each other underground

```{r tbl-subsurface-relation}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
gas_corrected <- analyze_fischer_gas_samples(con)
iso_raw <- DBI::dbGetQuery(con, "
  SELECT sample_label, d13c_permil, he3_he4_r_ra
  FROM Gas_Analyses
")
rel_tbl <- gas_corrected |>
  dplyr::left_join(iso_raw, by = "sample_label") |>
  dplyr::transmute(
    Sample = sample_label,
    `Field T (C)` = round(field_temp_c, 1),
    `CO2, air-corrected (%)` = round(CO2_corrected, 1),
    `H2S/CO2, air-corrected` = round(H2S_corrected / CO2_corrected, 3),
    `He R/Ra` = round(he3_he4_r_ra, 3),
    `d13C (permil)` = round(d13c_permil, 2),
    `D'Amore-Panichi T (C)` = round(dap_temperature_C, 0)
  )
knitr::kable(rel_tbl)
```

NV26-1 and NV26-2 both come from the fissure itself; NV26-3 is across
the road, a separate degassing spot. Setting NV26-2 aside for a
moment, since it's almost entirely air by the correction above and
therefore weak evidence either way, the real trend running from
NV26-1 to NV26-3 is a decline in both He R/Ra (5.989 to 5.600) and
D'Amore-Panichi temperature (228 C to 181 C), alongside a shift in
carbon isotope composition (d13C -8.28 to -9.161 permil, getting
slightly more negative).

I can read that two ways and I genuinely don't know which is right.
One reading is a single reservoir feeding both points, with
progressive cooling and/or dilution along whatever shared path the
gas takes to reach each vent -- the fissure vent being closer to the
"source" in some sense, the across-the-road vent being a bit further
along and a bit more diluted. The other reading is that these are two
separate vents tapping a similar but genuinely distinct source at
depth, and the small differences we're seeing are just that: two
different gas parcels that happen to look alike rather than one
parcel that evolved along the way. Three samples across two sites
isn't enough to tell those apart on its own, at least not with
anything I know how to do. Do you have an intuition, from other
systems you've worked on, for which of those two is more typical when
you see a gradient like this between two nearby vents -- and is there
a diagnostic (a ratio, an isotope system, something in the noble-gas
data we already have) that would actually distinguish them if we had
more samples?

**Water vs. gas geothermometry, and what the stacking actually
means.** Putting the gas geothermometer estimate next to our existing
water geothermometers (Na/K, quartz, chalcedony -- 148 estimates
across 67 real thermal samples) for the one point where we have both,
NV26-1's gas estimate (228 C) lands closest to the Na/K water
estimates (153-173 C), not the quartz/chalcedony ones (92-118 C).

```{r fig-geotherm-wg}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| results: asis
source(file.path(root, "scripts", "analysis", "geothermometer_water_gas_comparison.R"))
geo_path <- file.path(root, "output", "figures", "gas_analysis", "geothermometer_water_gas_comparison.png")
build_geothermometer_water_gas_figure(con, out_png = geo_path)
img3 <- gsub("\\\\", "/", normalizePath(geo_path))
knitr::asis_output(sprintf("![](%s)", img3))
```

We've shown this stacking before without really saying what it means,
so here's our actual read on it. Gas geothermometer hotter than Na/K,
Na/K hotter than quartz and chalcedony -- that ordering is the
classic signature of boiling and phase separation. When a thermal
fluid boils on its way up, gas partitions preferentially into the
vapor phase, and that vapor can carry a hotter, deeper equilibrium
signature with it even as the residual liquid keeps re-equilibrating
(and diluting) on the rest of the trip to the surface. That would
also explain quartz sitting below measured temperature -- silica
re-equilibrates fast and is tracking a shallower, cooler stage of the
same ascent than Na/K is. It's a tidy story and it fits, but it's our
working interpretation, not something we've tested against an
alternative. Is that the right read, or is there a simpler
explanation we're missing -- for instance, a known issue with running
D'Amore-Panichi on samples that needed this much air correction in
the first place?

## What kind of fumarole is this?

Worth asking plainly, since it bears on everything above: is this a
magmatic vent or something shallower? The gas is CO2-dominated with
only a few percent H2S, the field temperatures sit right around local
boiling (96-99.5 C, not superheated), and nothing in the geologic
literature we've got points to a shallow magma body under Steamboat.
Taken together, that reads to us as a peripheral, steam-heated
fumarole -- boiling of ascending thermal water near the surface,
rather than gas coming off a magmatic source directly. That's a fairly
ordinary call for a system like this, but it's also exactly the kind
of thing we'd rather have you confirm than assume. Does that
classification hold up, or is there something in the composition here
that argues against it?

## Deep source, shallow expression? Pulling it together

Stepping back, here's how we're currently reading the whole picture,
for what it's worth:

- Na/K (153-173 C) and the gas geothermometer (181-228 C) both point
  to a genuinely deep, hot reservoir underneath this system.
- Quartz and chalcedony (92-118 C), together with the measured vent
  temperature sitting right at local boiling, point to substantial
  cooling and/or dilution happening close to the surface.
- The He R/Ra (5.6-6.0) matches Torgersen and Jenkins' trusted 1982
  gas values (6.0) about as closely as two measurements 44 years apart
  could match, which reads to us as a deep, long-lived,
  mantle-influenced source that hasn't meaningfully changed in that
  time.

Put together, that's "deep source, shallow boiling expression" --
a hot, isotopically stable reservoir at depth, expressed at the
surface through a near-boiling, actively cooling and diluting flow
path. That's our synthesis from what we have so far, not a finding
we'd defend hard on three gas samples. Does that match how you'd read
it, or is there a piece of this that doesn't sit right to you?

We also ran a real PHREEQC gas-phase equilibration on this pairing,
described in detail below, and it complicates this picture a little
rather than confirming it cleanly -- worth reading before you weigh in
on the synthesis above.

```{r fig-gasphase-rup}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| results: asis
gp_path <- file.path(root, "output", "figures", "gas_analysis", "gas_phase_fischer_pairing_before_after.png")
img4 <- gsub("\\\\", "/", normalizePath(gp_path))
knitr::asis_output(sprintf("![](%s)", img4))
```

**The PHREEQC run, in more detail.** We went ahead and ran a real
PHREEQC `GAS_PHASE` equilibration rather than just talking about it in
the abstract. The setup: take SBF_0001's full measured water
chemistry (the May 1 water sample, co-located with NV26-1), and
re-equilibrate it against a gas phase seeded with NV26-1's real,
air-corrected CO2:H2S ratio -- about 96.5:3.5 -- at 1 atmosphere.
We treated it as an open system, meaning the gas phase is allowed to
keep resupplying itself rather than being a small, fixed pocket that
gets used up, on the assumption that the fissure is more like a
continuous vent than a sealed reservoir.

The result: pH drops from the water's measured 8.3 down to a modeled
6.3, and calcite, aragonite, and dolomite all flip from supersaturated
to undersaturated once the gas is added. That's a real, fairly large
shift, and it means the water as sampled isn't sitting in equilibrium
with the gas as sampled under the assumptions we used. The honest
question is what that actually tells us. It could mean the water and
gas genuinely aren't the same fluid parcel -- that gas and liquid
separate out at depth or on the way up, before either one reaches the
surface, which would actually support the boiling story above rather
than undercut it. Or it could mean our modeling choices are driving
the result more than the real chemistry is: 1 atm was a simplification
(we don't have a real estimate of the pressure this gas phase should
represent at depth), and the open-system assumption could be wrong in
either direction. I don't have the geochemical modeling background to
know which of those is doing more of the work here, and that's really
the core question I want your take on -- is a disequilibrium result
like this expected and unremarkable for a water and gas sampled two
days and some distance apart, or is it telling us something real about
how this system separates gas from liquid?

## How this fits into the rest of the thesis

This is the first real gas dataset the project has had, and it slots
into a few places we'd already scoped out but had no data for:

- The D'Amore-Panichi geothermometer code had only ever been run
  against your group's own historical numbers (Mariner & Janik) as a
  check -- this is the first time it's run on a Steamboat sample we
  actually collected ourselves.
- We'd had a PHREEQC gas-phase/mixing setup built for a while, waiting
  on a real dissolved-gas sample to test it against. NV26-1 is the
  first one, and the run above is already a real result, not just a
  working capability anymore.
- The NV26-1/SBF_0001 pairing is a natural input to the mixing-model
  chapter: a real gas end-member next to a real water end-member from
  (almost) the same spot, the same week.
- More broadly, it's a second, independent way to ask whether the
  system has cooled and diluted the way the water geochemistry already
  suggests -- which matters directly for the redistribution-vs-new-source
  question the poster raised.

## Questions for you

Mostly I want to make sure we're using and describing your group's
work correctly before any of this goes further, but a few of these
are genuinely open scientific questions where I'd value your read more
than anything else:

- How should we cite the gas analyses in the thesis, and separately
  if this turns into a conference abstract or paper -- Fischer's lab
  and Barry's lab specifically, or is there a preferred citation you'd
  want us to use?
- Is the air correction above a reasonable way to handle Giggenbach
  bottle samples collected this way, or does your group normally
  handle it differently, and should we match that instead?
- On the PHREEQC gas-phase run: is 1 atm/open-system a reasonable
  starting assumption, or is there a better estimate of the real
  pressure and volume this gas phase should represent at depth? And is
  the disequilibrium we got (pH and carbonate SI both shifting a lot)
  actually surprising, or is that about what you'd expect for a water
  and gas sampled two days and some distance apart rather than from
  the exact same parcel?
- On NV26-1 vs. NV26-3 (and setting NV26-2 aside): does the decline in
  He R/Ra and gas temperature between the two look to you like a
  single reservoir feeding both points with cooling/dilution along the
  way, or two separate vents on a similar-but-distinct source? Is
  there a ratio or isotope system in the data we already have that
  would actually distinguish those two possibilities?
- On the gas-over-water geothermometer stacking: does the
  boiling/phase-separation read we laid out above sound right to you,
  or is there a simpler explanation -- a known issue running
  D'Amore-Panichi on heavily air-corrected samples, for instance?
- Does "peripheral, steam-heated fumarole" sound like the right call
  for this vent, given the CO2-dominant, low-H2S composition and the
  near-boiling field temperatures, or is there something here that
  points toward (or against) a more direct magmatic connection?
- Does "deep, hot, isotopically stable source; shallow, boiling,
  diluting expression" match how you'd read this dataset, or do you
  see it differently?
- On the ternary plot: is the He-times-100/Ar-times-10 scaling I used
  the right convention, and is there a reference version of that
  diagram, with real air/crustal/mantle field boundaries, that we
  should be plotting these points against instead of just showing them
  relative to a single air point?
- On NV26-2: is the leak serious enough that the sample shouldn't be
  used at all, or is it still usable with the caveat we've got on it?
- Should we hold off on presenting any interpretation of the noble gas
  and carbon isotope numbers until you, Tobias, or Karim have had a
  chance to look at them yourselves, or is what's here reasonable to
  go forward with as a preliminary read?
- Would you, Tobias, and/or Karim want to be coauthors if this turns
  into a conference abstract or paper down the line?
